heading: One runtime, two workers
text: The sidecar is the entry worker. Anything outside /local-cf is forwarded to your worker over a service binding, which is how one port serves both. Binding identity is mirrored verbatim from your config onto the sidecar. That mirroring is the whole trick: Miniflare resolves two workers declaring the same databaseid to t

heading: The Node bridge
text: workerd cannot read the filesystem, see Miniflare's log stream, or restart the runtime — but the dashboard needs all three (migration files, the log tail, snapshot restore). Miniflare's function-form service bindings solve this without a second server: The sidecar calls env.BRIDGE.fetch(...) and lands directly in the N

text: Attach mode refuses writes because two workerd processes writing one set of SQLite files is not a supported configuration and has corrupted real projects. heading: Fidelity as data, not decoration
text: Every binding carries a fidelity field — live, disk, remote or unsupported — computed from the mode when the metadata is assembled, and rendered verbatim by the dashboard. This is the mechanism behind the project's central claim. It is what makes "attach mode is weaker than dev mode" a visible property of each binding

heading: Typed end to end
text: The sidecar is a Hono app; the dashboard consumes it with hc<ApiType: Query strings and JSON bodies are validated on the routes, which is what puts them into the client's signature — a typo is a build error, not a runtime surprise. A route without a validator cannot be called with a body through the typed client at all

text: The dashboard is a single page whose tabs are component state, not routes. That has one deliberate consequence: the same React tree builds twice — static-exported into the npm package for offline use, and compiled into this site's /app route by OpenNext — with no adapter layer between them. heading: local-cf attach (default)
text: Browse the persisted state of a dev server you do not control. Mode B. Read-only unless you pass --allow-write. This is the default command — running local-cf with no command runs attach. It never runs your worker, so it never needs to bundle it, which makes it the command most likely to just work on any project. It op

heading: local-cf dev
text: Run your worker and the studio in one runtime, read/write. Mode A. This is the full studio and the only mode where Durable Objects and Queues work. Requires a main entrypoint in your wrangler config — without one there is no worker to run, and local-cf will tell you to use attach instead.

heading: local-cf remote
text: Browse the real resources in your Cloudflare account over the REST API. Mode C. Requires credentials; see --account-id below. Covers D1, KV and R2. Durable Objects and Queues have no REST API equivalent.

heading: Before you start
text: You need: Node.js 20.11 or newer. Check with node --version. A Cloudflare Workers project with a wrangler.jsonc, wrangler.json or wrangler.toml in it. local-cf reads that file to discover your bindings — it is the only configuration it needs. You do not need a Cloudflare account, an API token, or an internet connection

heading: 1. Run it
text: Open a terminal in the directory containing your wrangler config and run: local-cf searches for a config file in that directory and then walks up through parent directories, the same way wrangler does. If it finds one, it prints a startup banner and a URL. Open the URL under studio in your browser. That's the setup.

text: Each line is worth knowing: | Line | Meaning | | --- | --- | | mode | Which of the three modes you are in | | access | Whether the studio will accept writes. read-only is the default for bare local-cf | | worker | The name from your wrangler config | | bundler | Only in dev mode. heading: The problem it solves

heading: The one idea worth understanding
text: Most tools that inspect local Workers data open the SQLite files themselves, from a separate process, and hope nothing changes underneath them. That is a copy of your data, one flush behind. local-cf can do something stronger. When it runs your worker itself, it starts a single workerd runtime containing two workers: y

heading: "Could not prepare a snapshot of the persist directory: every slot is locked"
text: Attach mode rotates through three copy slots under .local-cf/attached/. All three being locked means orphaned local-cf processes are still holding file handles — almost always on Windows, where an open handle makes a directory undeletable outright rather than merely stale. heading: Worker imports a .wasm module
text: Not supported yet. The built-in esbuild pass builds in memory, and emitting a separate wasm module needs an output path. If your project has wrangler installed, local-cf will try wrangler's bundler first — but a build that emits more than one module is rejected too, since side-modules would have to be wired into Minifl

text: You will see this in the banner and the logs: local-cf's runtime (workerd 1.20260730.1) is newer than your project's (workerd 1.20250109.0). Writing .wrangler/state with it can migrate those SQLite files in place and stop your own wrangler dev from starting. This is a real risk, not a formality. workerd migrates persis

heading: "local-cf is read-only in attach mode"
text: Working as intended. Bare npx local-cf runs attach mode, which is read-only because another dev server owns the persist directory, and two runtimes writing the same SQLite files can corrupt them. If you want to edit data, use the full studio: If your dev server is genuinely stopped and you want to edit what it left beh

heading: My SELECT works but my UPDATE doesn't
text: Also intended. The read-only guard exempts the SQL query route so that browsing keeps working, then checks each statement individually. Anything matching INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, ALTER, CREATE, REPLACE, TRUNCATE or PRAGMA is refused. Same two fixes as above.

heading: My data is stale / new writes don't appear
text: You are in attach mode, which reads a point-in-time copy taken when local-cf started. Data your dev server writes afterwards will not appear. Restart local-cf to take a fresh copy, or use local-cf dev for a live view. Bindings showing "on disk" rather than "live" in the dashboard are the ones affected.

heading: The dashboard shows a different database than my worker
text: Almost always a missing databaseid. Check the Overview tab for this warning: D1 binding "DB" has no databaseid; falling back to "my-database". Local storage identity is derived from this value… Local storage identity comes from databaseid. Without one, local-cf falls back to databasename and then to the binding name —

heading: A binding is missing from Overview
text: local-cf parses your config directly rather than through wrangler internals, and skips entries it cannot make sense of — each with a warning shown on the Overview tab. The usual causes: | Binding | Requires | | --- | --- | | d1databases | binding | | kvnamespaces | binding | | r2buckets | binding | | durableobjects.bin

heading: Durable Objects say "unavailable"
text: Expected outside local-cf dev. In attach mode there is no user worker in local-cf's runtime, so there is no class for a DO binding to point at. In remote mode there is no REST API for reading another Durable Object's storage. Run npx local-cf dev for live Durable Object access. Even in dev mode, you cannot browse a DO'

heading: Queue depth / dead letter contents are empty
text: Neither is observable from another worker in any mode. local-cf can send messages to producers and show your consumer's configuration, and in dev mode your consumer really runs — watch the Logs tab to see messages processed. But inspecting the queue itself is not possible.

heading: http://127.0.0.1:8787/ returns a 404
text: You are not in dev mode. Only local-cf dev runs your worker; attach and remote serve the studio alone. The 404 body says which mode you are in. The studio is always at /local-cf/ui/.
